cards.title: 4.1.1 Describing Acids
body: The sour taste of lemon and vinegar is due to the presence of different types of acids.
The same holds true for the sour taste of common fruits and vegetables.
HCl breaks down into H+ and Clions in an aqueous solution.

cards.title: Arrhenius theory, step by step
body: **Acid:** a substance that produces **hydrogen ions, H⁺**, in water. **Base:** a substance that produces **hydroxide ions, OH⁻**, in water.
HCl(aq) → H⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq); H₂SO₄(aq) → 2H⁺(aq) + SO₄²⁻(aq); NaOH(aq) → Na⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq).
**Neutralisation** is then simply H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → H₂O(l).

**Limitations:** (1) it works only in **water**; (2) it cannot explain why **ammonia, NH₃**, is a base — NH₃ contains no OH; (3) a bare H⁺ does not exist in water — it is attached to a water molecule as **H₃O⁺** (hydronium ion).

cards.title: Brønsted–Lowry theory, step by step
body: **Acid = proton (H⁺) donor. Base = proton (H⁺) acceptor.** An acid–base reaction is a **proton transfer**.
**Step 1 — Find which particle loses an H⁺.** That is the acid. HCl + H₂O → H₃O⁺ + Cl⁻: HCl loses H⁺ → acid; H₂O gains it → base.

**Step 2 — Find the conjugate pairs.** When an acid loses H⁺ it becomes its **conjugate base** (HCl → Cl⁻). When a base gains H⁺ it becomes its **conjugate acid** (H₂O → H₃O⁺). The two members of a pair differ by **exactly one H⁺**.
**Step 3 — Ammonia now makes sense:** NH₃ + H₂O ⇌ NH₄⁺ + OH⁻. NH₃ accepts H⁺ → base; H₂O donates H⁺ → acid.
**Amphiprotic (amphoteric) species** can act as acid or base: H₂O, HCO₃⁻, HSO₄⁻, H₂PO₄⁻.
**Strength rule:** the stronger the acid, the weaker its conjugate base (HCl is strong, Cl⁻ has almost no tendency to take H⁺ back).

cards.title: Lewis theory, step by step (extension)
body: The textbook covers Arrhenius and Brønsted–Lowry. The **Lewis** theory is the broadest and is met again in Grade 12 and university entrance questions:
**Lewis acid = electron-pair acceptor. Lewis base = electron-pair donor.** The product has a new **coordinate (dative) bond**.
**Step 1 — Look for a lone pair.** The particle that gives the lone pair is the base (NH₃, H₂O, OH⁻, F⁻, Cl⁻).
**Step 2 — Look for an empty orbital.** The particle that receives the pair is the acid (H⁺, BF₃, AlCl₃, metal ions such as Ag⁺, Cu²⁺, Fe³⁺).
**Example:** BF₃ + :NH₃ → F₃B←NH₃. BF₃ has only 6 electrons around B, so it accepts the pair; there is no proton at all, so only the Lewis theory calls this an acid–base reaction.
Every Brønsted base is also a Lewis base (it needs a lone pair to take an H⁺), and H⁺ itself is a Lewis acid.

cards.title: Model: the three theories side by side

steps.text: **Arrhenius** — in water: acids give H⁺, bases give OH⁻.
**Brønsted–Lowry** — the acid gives a proton to the base: HCl + H₂O → H₃O⁺ + Cl⁻.
**Lewis** — the base gives an electron pair to the acid: NH₃ → BF₃.

cards.title: Worked example: ammonia in water
cards.problem: For NH₃(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ NH₄⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq), identify the Brønsted acid, base and the two conjugate pairs.

steps.text: H₂O loses an H⁺ and becomes OH⁻ → H₂O is the **acid**, OH⁻ its **conjugate base**.
NH₃ gains an H⁺ and becomes NH₄⁺ → NH₃ is the **base**, NH₄⁺ its **conjugate acid**.
Pairs: H₂O/OH⁻ and NH₄⁺/NH₃. Each pair differs by one H⁺.
Arrhenius could not call NH₃ a base (it has no OH); Brønsted–Lowry can.

cards.answer: Acid H₂O, base NH₃; pairs H₂O/OH⁻ and NH₄⁺/NH₃.

cards.title: Worked example: HCO₃⁻ is amphiprotic
cards.problem: Show with equations that the hydrogen carbonate ion, HCO₃⁻, can act as both a Brønsted acid and a Brønsted base.

steps.text: As an **acid** (with OH⁻): HCO₃⁻ + OH⁻ → CO₃²⁻ + H₂O — it donates H⁺; conjugate base CO₃²⁻.
As a **base** (with H₃O⁺): HCO₃⁻ + H₃O⁺ → H₂CO₃ + H₂O — it accepts H⁺; conjugate acid H₂CO₃.
A species that can both donate and accept H⁺ is **amphiprotic**.

cards.answer: HCO₃⁻ donates H⁺ to OH⁻ and accepts H⁺ from H₃O⁺.

cards.title: Worked example: which theory fits?
cards.problem: Classify each reaction as acid–base under Arrhenius, Brønsted–Lowry and/or Lewis: (a) HCl(aq) + NaOH(aq) → NaCl(aq) + H₂O(l); (b) HCl(g) + NH₃(g) → NH₄Cl(s); (c) BF₃ + F⁻ → BF₄⁻.

steps.text: (a) In water, HCl gives H⁺ and NaOH gives OH⁻ → **Arrhenius**; H⁺ is transferred → **Brønsted**; OH⁻ gives a lone pair to H⁺ → **Lewis**. All three.
(b) No water, so not Arrhenius. HCl gives H⁺ to NH₃ → **Brønsted** (and Lewis).
(c) No proton is transferred. F⁻ donates an electron pair to BF₃ → **Lewis only**.

cards.answer: (a) all three; (b) Brønsted–Lowry and Lewis; (c) Lewis only.

cards.title: Step by step: Bases
body: **Step 1:** Arrhenius: a base produces OH⁻ ions in water (NaOH → Na⁺ + OH⁻); a soluble base is called an alkali.
**Step 2:** Brønsted–Lowry: a base is a proton (H⁺) acceptor: NH₃ + H₂O ⇌ NH₄⁺ + OH⁻.
**Step 3:** Properties: bitter taste, slippery feel, turn red litmus blue, phenolphthalein pink, pH above 7.
**Step 4:** Bases neutralize acids to form salt and water: NaOH + HCl → NaCl + H₂O; with ammonium salts they release ammonia gas.
**Step 5:** Strong bases ionize completely (NaOH, KOH); weak bases ionize partly (NH₃).
**Example:** Titration: 25.0 mL of NaOH is neutralized by 20.0 mL of 0.10 M HCl. n(HCl) = 0.10 × 0.0200 = 0.0020 mol = n(NaOH) (1 : 1). M(NaOH) = 0.0020 ÷ 0.0250 = 0.080 M.

cards.title: Describing a Neutralization Reaction
body: pH < 7 acid, 7 neutral, > 7 alkali. Each pH step is a ten-times change in [H⁺]. Indicators: litmus, methyl orange, phenolphthalein — pick one that flips near the end-point you want.

cards.title: 4.3.3 Indicators in a titration, step by step
body: An **acid–base indicator** is a dye (itself a weak acid or weak base) whose colour in its acid form differs from its colour in its base form. It changes colour as it **gains or loses H⁺ ions**, so it shows the **end point** of a titration.
**Step 1 — Fill the burette** with the solution of known concentration (e.g. NaOH). Read the starting volume at eye level, bottom of the meniscus.
**Step 2 — Pipette** an exact volume (e.g. 25.0 mL) of the other solution (e.g. HCl) into a conical flask.
**Step 3 — Add 2–3 drops of indicator.** Only a few drops: the indicator is itself a weak acid/base and too much would take part in the reaction.
**Step 4 — Run in the titrant** while swirling, quickly at first, then drop by drop near the end. A white tile under the flask helps you see the colour.
**Step 5 — Stop at the end point:** the first **permanent** colour change (e.g. colourless → pale pink with phenolphthalein).
**Step 6 — Read the final volume;** the difference is the titre. Repeat until two titres agree within 0.10 mL (concordant).

**End point vs equivalence point:** the **equivalence point** is when the acid and base have exactly reacted in the ratio of the equation; the **end point** is when the indicator changes colour. A good indicator makes the two almost the same.

steps.text: **Burette** holds the titrant (e.g. 0.100 M NaOH); read volumes at the bottom of the meniscus.
**Conical flask** holds the pipetted acid with 2–3 drops of indicator; swirl so the drops mix at once.
**End point:** the first permanent pale pink with phenolphthalein. Stop and read the burette.

cards.why:
A **normal salt** is formed when all the replaceable hydrogen atoms of an acid are completely replaced by a metal or ammonium ion. 

- $$ HCl $$ (monoprotic) forms $$ NaCl $$.
- $$ H_2SO_4 $$ (diprotic) forms $$ Na_2SO_4 $$.
- $$ H_2CO_3 $$ (diprotic) forms $$ Na_2CO_3 $$.
- $$ H_3PO_4 $$ (triprotic) forms $$ Na_3PO_4 $$.

Since all these acids can have all their hydrogens replaced, they all produce normal salts.

cards.title: Salts
body: Salt = acid H replaced by a metal/ammonium. Prepare: metal + acid, carbonate + acid, base + acid, precipitation for insolubles.

cards.title: Lab pattern for salts
body: Soluble salt from a metal, base or carbonate: add the solid to warm acid until some remains (acid is used up), filter off the extra solid, evaporate until crystals form, cool, filter, dry. Excess solid method avoids leftover acid in the crystals. Insoluble salt: mix two solutions that swap partners, filter, wash, dry — precipitation.

Titration hygiene: rinse pipette with the solution it will measure, burette with the other, conical flask with distilled water only (you will add a known volume next). Repeat to concordant titres. Indicator choice: strong acid / strong base — almost any; weak acid / strong base — phenolphthalein.
pH is a log scale. Jumping from 4 to 3 is not “a bit more acid” — it is ten times the [H⁺]. Universal indicator is a rainbow estimate; a pH meter is a number.

cards.title: 4.4.4 Preparing salts, step by step
body: A salt contains the **positive ion of a base (or metal)** and the **negative ion of an acid**. Choose the method from **two questions**: Is the salt soluble in water? Which starting materials are safe and available?
**Method 1 — Neutralisation (acid + alkali).** For soluble salts of Na, K and NH₄. Titrate to find the exact volumes, mix again without indicator, evaporate and crystallise.
$$\mathrm{NaOH(aq)} + \mathrm{HCl(aq)} \rightarrow \mathrm{NaCl(aq)} + \mathrm{H_{2}O(l)}$$
**Method 2 — Acid + metal.** Only metals **more reactive than hydrogen** and not too reactive (Mg, Zn, Fe). Not Cu or Ag (no reaction); never Na or K (explosive).
$$\mathrm{Mg(s)} + \mathrm{H_{2}SO_{4}(aq)} \rightarrow \mathrm{MgSO_{4}(aq)} + \mathrm{H_{2}(g)}$$
**Method 3 — Acid + carbonate or hydrogencarbonate.** Fizzing shows CO₂.
$$\mathrm{BaCO_{3}(s)} + 2\mathrm{HCl(aq)} \rightarrow \mathrm{BaCl_{2}(aq)} + \mathrm{H_{2}O(l)} + \mathrm{CO_{2}(g)}$$
$$\mathrm{HNO_{3}(aq)} + \mathrm{NaHCO_{3}(aq)} \rightarrow \mathrm{NaNO_{3}(aq)} + \mathrm{H_{2}O(l)} + \mathrm{CO_{2}(g)}$$
**Method 4 — Acid + insoluble base (metal oxide), Activity 4.8.** Black CuO dissolves in warm dilute sulphuric acid to give a **blue** solution of copper(II) sulphate.
$$\mathrm{CuO(s)} + \mathrm{H_{2}SO_{4}(aq)} \rightarrow \mathrm{CuSO_{4}(aq)} + \mathrm{H_{2}O(l)}$$

**For methods 2–4 (excess solid):** add the solid to warm acid until no more dissolves (the acid is used up) → **filter** off the excess → **evaporate** to a saturated solution → **cool to crystallise** → filter and dry the crystals.
**Method 5 — Precipitation (double decomposition)** for **insoluble** salts: mix two solutions that contain the two ions, filter, wash with distilled water, dry.
$$\mathrm{BaCl_{2}(aq)} + \mathrm{Na_{2}SO_{4}(aq)} \rightarrow \mathrm{BaSO_{4}(s)} + 2\mathrm{NaCl(aq)}$$
**(Extra) Direct combination** of a metal and a non-metal: 2Na(s) + Cl₂(g) → 2NaCl(s); Fe(s) + S(s) → FeS(s).

cards.title: 4.5.1 Measuring pH
body: Measuring the pH of a swimming pool is important: if the pH is outside the safe range (about 7.2–7.8) it can irritate the skin and allow bacteria to grow.
A universal indicator shows a series of colour changes at different pH values, so it indicates how acidic or alkaline the solution under investigation is.

cards.title: 4.5.1 Measuring pH, step by step
body: There are two common ways to measure pH: a **pH meter** and **indicators**. We measure pH in daily life too — for example swimming-pool water must stay at about pH 7.2–7.8, or it irritates skin and lets bacteria grow.

**A · The pH meter (accurate, a number):** a pair of electrodes (a glass probe) is connected to a meter that measures a small voltage. The voltage depends on [H⁺], and the meter is calibrated to show pH.
1. **Calibrate** with buffer solutions of known pH (e.g. pH 4 and 7).
2. **Rinse** the probe with distilled water and dip it into the sample.
3. **Wait** for a steady reading and record it (e.g. pH 6.84).
4. **Rinse** again before the next sample and store the probe wet.

**B · Indicators (quick, a colour, less precise):** an indicator has one colour in acid and another in base and changes within a small pH range. Many come from plants: red cabbage, roses, beetroot, grapes, sunflower petals. They are used as solutions or soaked onto paper.
**C · Universal indicator** is a **mixture** of indicators, so it shows a different colour for each pH value. Compare the colour with the chart to estimate the pH.

steps.text: **Colours (textbook Table 4.7):** pH 1–4 red, 5 orange, 6 yellow, 7 green, 8 bluish-green, 9 blue, 10 bluish-purple, 11–14 purple.
**Everyday values:** lemon juice ≈ 2–3, coffee ≈ 5, milk ≈ 6.5, blood ≈ 7.4, baking soda ≈ 8–9, bleach ≈ 12–13.

cards.title: Step by step: The pH scale
body: **Step 1:** pH measures acidity: pH = −log[H⁺]. The scale runs from 0 to 14 at 25 °C.
**Step 2:** pH < 7 acidic, pH = 7 neutral (pure water), pH > 7 basic (alkaline).
**Step 3:** Each unit of pH is a factor of 10 in [H⁺]: pH 3 is ten times more acidic than pH 4.
**Step 4:** pH + pOH = 14, where pOH = −log[OH⁻].
**Step 5:** Measure pH with universal indicator (colour chart), pH paper or a pH meter (most accurate).
**Example:** [H⁺] = 1 × 10⁻³ M → pH = 3 (acidic). A 0.01 M NaOH solution: [OH⁻] = 10⁻² → pOH = 2 → pH = 14 − 2 = 12 (basic).

why: Step 1: HNO₃ loses H⁺ → acid; it becomes NO₃⁻ (conjugate base).

questions.tip: Track the H⁺: who loses it, who gains it.

similar.q: Identify the pairs in CH₃COOH + H₂O ⇌ CH₃COO⁻ + H₃O⁺.
In CO₃²⁻ + H₂O ⇌ HCO₃⁻ + OH⁻, which is the base?

questions.label: 4.1 Acid–base theories

questions.q: Which species is amphiprotic?
why: Step 1: amphiprotic = can donate and accept H⁺.
Step 2: HCO₃⁻ can lose H⁺ (→ CO₃²⁻) or gain H⁺ (→ H₂CO₃).
questions.tip: Look for an ion that still has an H and a negative charge (HCO₃⁻, HSO₄⁻, H₂PO₄⁻) — or water.

similar.q: Give the conjugate acid of HSO₄⁻.

questions.label: 4.1 Acid–base theories

questions.q: Every Arrhenius acid is also a Brønsted–Lowry acid.
why: Step 1: an Arrhenius acid releases H⁺ in water.
Step 2: releasing H⁺ means donating a proton (to water).
Step 3: so it is also a Brønsted acid; the reverse is not always true.
questions.tip: Each newer theory contains the older one.

similar.q: Is every Lewis acid a Brønsted acid?
similar.a: No — BF₃ is a Lewis acid with no proton.

similar.q: Which theory explains NH₃ as a base?

questions.label: 4.1 Acid–base theories

questions.q: Explain why AlCl₃ is called a Lewis acid.
questions.answer: Al in AlCl₃ has only 6 outer electrons and an empty orbital, so it accepts an electron pair (e.g. from Cl⁻ or NH₃).
why: Step 1: Al has 3 valence electrons; with three Cl it has 6 around it.
Step 2: it has room for one more pair.
Step 3: accepting an electron pair = Lewis acid.
questions.tip: Electron-deficient central atom → Lewis acid.

similar.q: Is NH₃ a Lewis acid or base?
Why is H⁺ a Lewis acid?
similar.a: It has an empty orbital and accepts a lone pair.

questions.label: 4.1 Acid–base theories

questions.q: Which indicator is best for titrating ammonia solution with hydrochloric acid?
why: Step 1: NH₃ is a weak base; HCl is a strong acid.
Step 2: the salt NH₄Cl makes the solution slightly acidic at equivalence (pH ≈ 5).
Step 3: methyl orange changes in the acid range (3.1–4.4) → best.
questions.tip: Weak base → methyl orange.
questions.label: 4.3.3 Using indicators in a titration

questions.q: 20.0 mL of 0.150 M HCl is neutralised by 30.0 mL of KOH. Find the molarity of the KOH.
why: Step 1: HCl + KOH → KCl + H₂O (1 : 1).
Step 3: moles KOH = 3.00 × 10⁻³ mol.
questions.tip: Moles first, then use the mole ratio.

similar.q: Volume of 0.10 M NaOH for 25 mL of 0.10 M HCl?

questions.label: 4.3.3 Using indicators in a titration

questions.q: Phenolphthalein is added to HCl in a flask and NaOH is run in. The colour change at the end point is …
why: Step 1: in acid phenolphthalein is colourless.
Step 2: the first slight excess of NaOH makes the solution basic.
Step 3: phenolphthalein turns pink.
questions.tip: Think “from what is in the flask to what is added”.

similar.q: Methyl orange, base in the flask, acid added?
Phenolphthalein, NaOH in the flask, HCl added?

questions.label: 4.3.3 Using indicators in a titration

questions.q: Which acid and which base would you use to prepare (a) MgCl₂, (b) CaSO₄, (c) KBr? (Exercise 4.4 Q2)
questions.answer: (a) Mg(OH)₂ (or MgO) + HCl; (b) Ca(OH)₂ + H₂SO₄; (c) KOH + HBr.
why: Step 1: the metal ion of the salt comes from the base.
Step 2: the negative ion comes from the acid: chloride ← HCl, sulphate ← H₂SO₄, bromide ← HBr.
Step 3: e.g. Mg(OH)₂ + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + 2H₂O.
questions.tip: Split the salt name: first part → base, second part → acid.
questions.label: 4.3.3 Using indicators in a titration

questions.q: At the end point of every acid–base titration the pH is exactly 7.
why: Step 1: pH 7 at equivalence only for strong acid + strong base.
Step 2: weak acid + strong base gives pH ≈ 9; strong acid + weak base pH ≈ 5.
Step 3: so the statement is false.
questions.tip: The salt formed decides the pH at equivalence.

similar.q: pH at equivalence for CH₃COOH + NaOH?

questions.label: 4.3.3 Using indicators in a titration

questions.q: Why is litmus not used as an indicator in titrations?
questions.answer: Its colour changes gradually over a wide pH range (5–8) through purple, so the end point is not sharp.
why: Step 1: a good indicator changes sharply with one drop.
Step 2: litmus passes slowly from red through purple to blue.
Step 3: it is hard to see exactly when to stop.
questions.tip: A sharp change = a precise end point.
questions.label: 4.3.3 Using indicators in a titration

questions.q: Which pair would react to give zinc chloride and hydrogen?
why: Step 1: hydrogen is produced only by metal + acid.
Step 2: Zn is above H in the activity series.
Step 3: Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂. ZnO gives water; ZnCO₃ gives CO₂.
questions.tip: Metal + acid → salt + hydrogen.
questions.label: 4.4.4 Methods for preparing salts

questions.q: Write the balanced equation, with state symbols, for making magnesium nitrate from magnesium carbonate.
why: Step 1: nitrate → nitric acid.
Step 2: carbonate + acid → salt + water + carbon dioxide.
Step 3: Mg²⁺ needs two NO₃⁻ → 2HNO₃.
Step 4: check H 2 = 2, O 9 = 9.
questions.tip: Carbonate + acid always gives CO₂ and water.
questions.label: 4.4.4 Methods for preparing salts

questions.q: Silver chloride is best prepared by …
why: Step 1: AgCl is insoluble.
Step 2: insoluble salts are made by precipitation.
Step 3: AgNO₃(aq) + NaCl(aq) → AgCl(s) + NaNO₃(aq); filter, wash, dry.
questions.tip: Insoluble → precipitation.

similar.q: Which salt is insoluble: AgCl or AgNO₃?

questions.label: 4.4.4 Methods for preparing salts

questions.q: List the steps to obtain pure crystals of zinc sulphate from zinc and dilute sulphuric acid.
questions.answer: Add excess zinc to the acid until fizzing stops; filter off unreacted zinc; evaporate the filtrate to the point of crystallisation; cool; filter and dry the crystals.
why: Step 1: Zn(s) + H₂SO₄(aq) → ZnSO₄(aq) + H₂(g).
Step 2: excess zinc makes sure all the acid reacts (fizzing stops).
Step 3: filter to remove the extra zinc.
Step 4: evaporate to saturation, cool, collect and dry the crystals.
questions.tip: Excess → filter → evaporate → crystallise.
questions.label: 4.4.4 Methods for preparing salts

questions.q: Sodium chloride can safely be made by adding sodium metal to hydrochloric acid.
why: Step 1: sodium is very reactive.
Step 2: with acid the reaction is violent (explosive) and dangerous.
Step 3: NaCl is made by titrating NaOH with HCl.
questions.tip: Very reactive metals (Na, K) and unreactive metals (Cu, Ag) are not used with acids.

similar.q: Can copper be used with dilute HCl?

questions.label: 4.4.4 Methods for preparing salts

questions.q: What do you observe when copper(II) oxide is added to warm dilute sulphuric acid (Activity 4.8)? Write the equation.
questions.answer: The black powder dissolves and the colourless acid turns blue (copper(II) sulphate). CuO(s) + H₂SO₄(aq) → CuSO₄(aq) + H₂O(l).
why: Step 1: CuO is a black basic oxide.
Step 2: it neutralises the acid to form soluble CuSO₄, which is blue.
Step 3: when excess CuO is added, black solid remains undissolved.
questions.tip: Copper(II) salts in solution are blue.
questions.label: 4.4.4 Methods for preparing salts

questions.q: A solution turns universal indicator purple. It is …
why: Step 1: purple is at pH 11–14 on the chart.
Step 2: pH far above 7 → strongly alkaline.
Step 3: e.g. NaOH solution or bleach.
questions.tip: Red end = acid, purple end = alkali.
questions.label: 4.5.1 Measuring pH

questions.q: Calculate the pH of a solution with [H⁺] = 3.0 × 10⁻⁴ M.
why: Step 1: pH = −log(3.0 × 10⁻⁴).
Step 4: below 7 → acidic.
questions.tip: pH = −log[H⁺]; for a×10⁻ⁿ the pH is a little below n.
questions.label: 4.5.1 Measuring pH

questions.q: Which is the most accurate way to measure the pH of soil water?
why: Step 1: indicators give colours (ranges).
Step 2: a calibrated pH meter gives a numerical value.
Step 3: so the pH meter is most accurate.
questions.tip: Number beats colour.

similar.q: What must be done before using a pH meter?

questions.label: 4.5.1 Measuring pH

questions.q: Estimate the pH of orange juice, milk, blood and bleach, and say which is the most acidic. (Exercise 4.7 Q2b)
questions.answer: Orange juice ≈ 3–4, milk ≈ 6.5, blood ≈ 7.4, bleach ≈ 12–13; orange juice is the most acidic.
why: Step 1: fruit juices contain citric acid → pH 3–4.
Step 2: milk is close to neutral, slightly acidic (≈ 6.5).
Step 3: blood is slightly alkaline (7.35–7.45).
Step 4: bleach (NaOCl + NaOH) is strongly alkaline; the lowest pH is the most acidic → orange juice.
questions.tip: Lower pH = more acidic.
questions.label: 4.5.1 Measuring pH

questions.q: A solution of pH 4 has ten times more H⁺ ions than a solution of pH 5.
why: Step 1: [H⁺] at pH 4 = 10⁻⁴ M; at pH 5 = 10⁻⁵ M.
Step 3: true.
questions.tip: One pH unit = ×10.

similar.q: pH 9 vs pH 7: more or less H⁺?
